title: How to work cross-stitch over two threads on evenweave
subtitle: Placing each stitch over two warp and two weft threads for a consistent grid
excerpt: Cross-stitch on evenweave linen or Jobelan fabric is worked over two threads in each direction. The stitch spans two warp threads horizontally and two weft threads vertically, creating a square cross on the fabric surface. The stitching process is the same as on Aida, but the counting method is different because the fabric has no pre-formed holes.
sourceNotes: Cross-stitch over two threads on evenweave linen. Weldon's Practical Needlework series (1880s), Internet Archive. Standard guidance in major cross-stitch publisher guides.

glossaryTerms.definition: The six-strand embroidery thread used for cross-stitch.
A stiff, evenly-woven cross-stitch fabric with clearly visible squares formed by groups of threads.

content.text: Working over two threads on evenweave gives the same visual result as

but on a softer, more translucent fabric. The stitches are placed between specific warp and weft threads rather than in pre-formed holes, so counting is the critical skill. Each cross covers exactly two threads in both the horizontal and vertical directions.
Mount the evenweave in a hoop or scroll frame at firm tension. Evenweave is softer than Aida and needs consistent tension to prevent distortion during stitching.

Identify the start position for the first stitch. Count from a corner or centre reference point, moving in units of two threads along the warp and weft. The needle always enters and exits the fabric between threads, not through them; use a blunt tapestry needle.

Bring the needle up between threads at the lower-left corner of the first stitch square. This position should be between the 2nd and 3rd weft thread from the bottom of the square and between the 2nd and 3rd warp thread from the left.
Insert the needle between the threads two warp and two weft threads diagonally up and to the right, creating the first diagonal leg of the cross. Pull the
snug but not tight. The leg should span exactly two threads in each direction and lie flat against the fabric.

Complete the cross by working the return diagonal: from lower-right to upper-left over the same two-by-two span. The completed cross should be square and the thread should sit smooth on the fabric surface without any puckering.

Move to the next stitch position by counting two threads along the fabric. The even spacing between stitches should be consistent across the whole design; check periodically by counting back to the first stitch position.

items.symptom: The stitches are not square — some crosses look longer in one direction
items.cause: The thread count was inconsistent; some stitches span two threads in one direction and three in the other.
items.fix: Count carefully at every stitch. On 28-count evenweave this is easy to check by holding the fabric up to light; the thread spacing is visible. Unpick any non-square stitches and re-work them over the correct two-by-two span.

items.symptom: The needle is splitting the evenweave threads rather than passing between them
items.cause: A sharp needle is piercing the fine threads of the evenweave.
items.fix: Switch to a blunt tapestry needle. The rounded tip pushes between threads without splitting them. On fine evenweave, a size 26 or 28 tapestry needle is appropriate for 2-strand work.

content.text: The same chart used on 14-count Aida can be used on 28-count evenweave worked over two threads; the stitch count and spacing are identical, but the fabric background is softer and the stitches have a slightly different character on the finer ground. Many stitchers who have worked on Aida for some time find evenweave a natural next step.
